{{DISPLAYTITLE:Proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Two kinds of equality}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Two rules govern how proofs behave in Lean. '''Definitional proof irrelevance''' makes any
two proofs of the same proposition definitionally equal. '''Restricted elimination''' allows
a proof to be taken apart to produce data only when the proposition is a
'''subsingleton''', one that by its shape can have at most one proof. The first rule says
that the content of a proof never matters; the second is what keeps that consistent. This
page states both rules, lists which propositions pass the test, explains why the test is
needed, and sets out the cost: together with the accessibility predicate, the two rules make
Lean's definitional equality undecidable.

== Definitional proof irrelevance ==

Carneiro's presentation of Lean's type theory includes the rule<ref name="carneiro">Mario Carneiro, ''The Type Theory of Lean'', Master's thesis, Carnegie Mellon University, 2019; §2.2 (pp. 6–7), §2.6.2 (pp. 10–11), §2.6.4 (p. 12), §2.8 (p. 15), §3.1 (pp. 16–17), Lemma 3.4 (pp. 18–19) and Corollary 6.8 (p. 41). https://github.com/digama0/lean-type-theory/releases/tag/v1.0</ref>

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash p : \mathrm{Prop} \quad \Gamma \vdash h : p \quad \Gamma \vdash h' : p}{\Gamma \vdash h \equiv h'}</math>

It is a rule of definitional equality, so the checker applies it during conversion, without
any proof term. The reference manual lists it among the defining properties of
<code>Prop</code>, beside the erasure of propositions from compiled code.<ref name="refman-props">''The Lean Language Reference'', version 4.34.0, §4.2 "Propositions". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Propositions/</ref>

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example (p : Prop) (h₁ h₂ : p) : h₁ = h₂ := rfl

example (h₁ h₂ : 0 &lt; 5) : (⟨5, h₁⟩ : {n : Nat // 0 &lt; n}) = ⟨5, h₂⟩ := rfl

example (α : Type) (h₁ h₂ : Nonempty α) : Classical.choice h₁ = Classical.choice h₂ := rfl
</pre>

All three are accepted. The second shows the practical use: elements of a subtype are equal
as soon as their values are, whatever proofs they carry. The third shows that global choice
returns one element per type, not one per proof. Carneiro, writing in 2019, notes that Coq
then had proof irrelevance only as an axiom asserting a propositional equality, and calls
Lean's definitional version "a major departure for the theory".<ref name="carneiro" />

== Why elimination must be restricted ==

Suppose a program could inspect which constructor built a proof of a disjunction, and so
return <code>true</code> on <code>Or.inl trivial : True ∨ True</code> and <code>false</code>
on <code>Or.inr trivial</code>. Those two proofs have the same type, so proof irrelevance
makes them definitionally equal, the two results would be definitionally equal, and
<code>true = false</code> would follow by <code>rfl</code>. One of the two rules has to
give way. Lean keeps proof irrelevance and forbids the inspection: having been given a
proof, a program must not be able to tell which proof it received.<ref name="refman-ind">''The Lean Language Reference'', version 4.34.0, §4.4 "Inductive Types", subsection "Subsingleton Elimination". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Inductive-Types/#subsingleton-elimination</ref>
Lean refuses the function:

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def which (h : True ∨ True) : Bool :=
  match h with
  | .inl _ => true
  | .inr _ => false
</pre>

The message begins <code>Tactic `cases` failed with a nested error:</code> and continues
<code>Tactic `induction` failed: recursor `Or.casesOn` can only eliminate into `Prop`</code>.
The restriction is visible in the recursors themselves. The motive of <code>Or.rec</code>
and of <code>Exists.rec</code> returns <code>Prop</code>, while the motives of
<code>True.rec</code>, <code>False.rec</code> and <code>And.rec</code> return an arbitrary
<code>Sort u_1</code>:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#check @True.rec
#check @False.rec
#check @And.rec
#check @Or.rec
#check @Exists.rec
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
@True.rec : {motive : True → Sort u_1} → motive True.intro → (t : True) → motive t
False.rec : (motive : False → Sort u_1) → (t : False) → motive t
@And.rec : {a b : Prop} → {motive : a ∧ b → Sort u_1} → ((left : a) → (right : b) → motive ⋯) → (t : a ∧ b) → motive t
@Or.rec : ∀ {a b : Prop} {motive : a ∨ b → Prop},
  (∀ (h : a), motive ⋯) → (∀ (h : b), motive ⋯) → ∀ (t : a ∨ b), motive t
@Exists.rec : ∀ {α : Sort u_1} {p : α → Prop} {motive : Exists p → Prop},
  (∀ (w : α) (h : p w), motive ⋯) → ∀ (t : Exists p), motive t
</pre>

== The rule ==

An inductive type in <code>Prop</code> may be eliminated into any universe, which is
'''large elimination''', when it is a syntactic subsingleton. The reference manual states
the test as two conditions: there is at most one constructor, and every argument of that
constructor either has a proposition as its type or is a parameter or an index of the
type.<ref name="refman-ind" /> Carneiro's formulation is that there is at most one constructor
and every non-recursive argument of it either has a proposition as its type or appears
directly in the constructor's output type.<ref name="carneiro" /> Otherwise the motive of the recursor must return
<code>Prop</code>. The test is deliberately conservative: it does not ask for a proof that
the proposition has at most one proof, only for a shape that guarantees it.<ref name="refman-ind" />

The standard cases:

* '''<code>True</code>''' has one constructor with no arguments, and '''<code>False</code>''' has none. From <code>h : False</code>, <code>h.elim</code> produces an element of any type.<ref name="refman-ind" />
* '''<code>And</code>''' has one constructor whose arguments are proofs.<ref name="refman-ind" />
* '''<code>Eq</code>''' has one constructor, <code>Eq.refl a</code>, whose argument is fixed by the type's parameters. This is why a proof of an equation can rewrite the type of data, the operation called transport on [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Propositional equality|propositional equality]].<ref name="refman-ind" />
* '''<code>Acc</code>''', the accessibility predicate, has one constructor <code>Acc.intro x h</code>. Its argument <code>x</code> appears in the result type <code>Acc r x</code> and its argument <code>h</code> is a proof, so it too eliminates into any universe. Carneiro singles it out as the source of proof by well-founded recursion.<ref name="carneiro" />

<code>Or</code> fails because it has two constructors. <code>Exists</code> and
<code>Nonempty</code> fail because their constructor stores a witness that is neither a
proof nor part of the type. Their proofs therefore cannot yield the witness as data; that
requires <code>Classical.choose</code>, as on
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Classical logic from choice|classical logic from choice]].
Where the witness is wanted as data, the subtype <code>{x // p x}</code>, which lives in
<code>Type</code>, carries it.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
def fromFalse (h : False) : Nat := h.elim

def castAlong {α β : Type} (h : α = β) (x : α) : β := h ▸ x

def bothThen {p q : Prop} (h : p ∧ q) (f : p → q → Nat) : Nat :=
  match h with
  | ⟨hp, hq⟩ => f hp hq

set_option pp.proofs true in
#check @Acc.rec
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
@Acc.rec : {α : Sort u_2} →
  {r : α → α → Prop} →
    {motive : (a : α) → Acc r a → Sort u_1} →
      ((x : α) →
          (h : ∀ (y : α), r y x → Acc r y) → ((y : α) → (a : r y x) → motive y (h y a)) → motive x (Acc.intro x h)) →
        {a : α} → (t : Acc r a) → motive a t
</pre>

For subsingletons the checker also applies an extra reduction, which Carneiro calls K-like
reduction: by proof irrelevance the major premise may be replaced by the constructor, and
the ordinary computation rule then fires. It applies only when every argument of the
constructor can be read off the type, which is the reason for the shape of the
test.<ref name="carneiro" /> For <code>Eq</code> it makes transport along any proof of
<code>a = a</code> reduce to the identity.

== The cost: definitional equality is undecidable ==

Proof irrelevance and the large eliminator of <code>Acc</code> together break the
decidability of definitional equality. Carneiro's argument runs as follows.<ref name="carneiro" />
From a proof <code>a : Acc r x</code> one can project, with the eliminator, a function
giving accessibility of every smaller element; call it <code>a.inv</code>. Rebuilding with
the constructor gives a proof of the same proposition, so by proof irrelevance
<code>a</code> and <code>Acc.intro x a.inv</code> are definitionally equal:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
example {α : Sort u} {r : α → α → Prop} {x : α} (a : Acc r x) :
    a = Acc.intro x (fun _ h => a.inv h) := rfl
</pre>

That step turns any proof, even an opaque variable, into a constructor on which the
recursor can compute. Now take a decidable predicate <math>P</math> on the natural
numbers, such as "machine <math>M</math> runs for at least <math>n</math> steps without
halting", and a function <math>f</math> defined by recursion on <code>Acc</code> for the
relation <math>></math>, which at <math>n</math> returns a fixed value if
<math>P(n)</math> fails and otherwise calls itself at <math>n+1</math>. The relation
<math>></math> on the natural numbers is not well founded, so a hypothesis
<math>a : \mathrm{Acc}\,(>)\,0</math> is unprovable, but definitional equality is
judged in every context, inconsistent ones included. In that context each use of the
equation above lets <math>f\,0\,a</math> take one more step of the search. If
<math>P(n)</math> fails for some <math>n</math>, the search ends and <math>f\,0\,a</math> is
definitionally equal to the fixed value; if <math>P</math> holds everywhere, every term
definitionally equal to <math>f\,0\,a</math> still contains a call of <math>f</math>.
Deciding that one definitional equality would decide whether <math>M</math> halts.

Lean's checker cannot implement an undecidable relation. It implements a decidable
approximation, which Carneiro calls algorithmic equality, and the two must differ: the
chain of equalities above holds step by step, but the checker, which does not perform the
"creative" re-expansion of a normal term, does not relate its two ends. Algorithmic
equality is therefore not transitive.<ref name="carneiro" /> The reference manual records
the same fact: definitional equality as Lean checks it is reflexive and symmetric, but not
transitive.<ref name="refman-ts">''The Lean Language Reference'', version 4.34.0, §4 "The Type System" (definitional equality). https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/</ref> Carneiro also shows that, measured against the
algorithmic relation, typing fails subject reduction: a term can be well typed and reduce
to one that the checker rejects.<ref name="carneiro" />

None of this lets the checker accept a false theorem. Algorithmic equality implies the
ideal definitional equality for well-typed terms, so whatever the checker accepts is
derivable in the theory; Carneiro uses exactly this step in his consistency proof. The
defect is incompleteness, not unsoundness.<ref name="carneiro" />
Abel and Coquand later showed a related failure: with an impredicative <code>Prop</code>
and proof-irrelevant equality, reduction need not terminate at all.<ref name="abel-coquand">Andreas Abel and Thierry Coquand, "Failure of normalization in impredicative type theory with proof-irrelevant propositional equality", ''Logical Methods in Computer Science'' 16(2) (2020), paper 14. https://doi.org/10.23638/LMCS-16(2:14)2020</ref>
That result, and why the checker remains sound regardless, are treated on
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Consistency and the metatheory|consistency and the metatheory]].
Abel and Coquand also note the other design: Agda and Coq had recently gained a proof-irrelevant universe
of strict propositions in which equality can be defined but cannot be eliminated into types
that are not themselves strict propositions, and under that restriction normalisation and
decidable type checking have been proved for the predicative case.<ref name="abel-coquand" />
